title: Composting Myths and Microbes
content:
Compost looks quiet from the outside, but it is a busy, breathable ecosystem. The difference between a sweet, earthy pile and a slimy mess usually comes down to two basics: air and balance. Once you understand the microbes doing the work, you can steer the process instead of guessing.

Two common myths trip people up. First, compost does not need magic starters or special powders. Second, it should not stink. If it smells like rotten eggs or sour trash, the pile is telling you it is low on oxygen or drowned in wet material.

Meet the microbes

Bacteria are the first responders, breaking down sugars and proteins and creating the first heat. Fungi move in when tougher fibers remain, while actinomycetes work on woody bits and give mature compost its earthy smell. Larger helpers like beetles, worms, and sow bugs do not do the chemistry, but they shred and aerate the pile so microbes can keep working.

Greens, browns, and rough ratios

Think in textures, not exact math. Greens bring nitrogen and moisture, while browns bring carbon and structure. A simple starting point is one bucket of greens to two or three buckets of browns by volume.

  • Greens: fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, fresh grass clippings, green weeds.
  • Browns: dried leaves, straw, shredded paper, cardboard, wood chips.
  • Avoid: meat, dairy, oily foods, and pet waste, which attract pests and slow the process.

Build a pile that can breathe

Aeration is the secret ingredient. A pile that can breathe will heat, shrink, and smell like soil. Aim for a minimum size of about 3 feet by 3 feet by 3 feet so the center can warm, but do not pack it tight.

  1. Lay a 4 to 6 inch base of twigs or coarse browns to keep the bottom airy.
  2. Alternate 2 to 4 inch layers of greens and browns, moistening as you go.
  3. Sprinkle a thin layer of finished compost or garden soil to introduce microbes.
  4. Cap the pile with dry browns to reduce flies and odors.

Moisture and oxygen

The best moisture check is the squeeze test. Grab a handful from the center and squeeze hard. You should get only a drop or two of water. If it drips, add browns and turn. If it crumbles into dust, add water and more greens.

If you can squeeze a handful and get only a drop or two, you are in the zone.

Temperature and timing

A hot pile runs between 130 and 160 degrees F for a few days, then cools as food runs out. Turning the pile every one to two weeks recharges it with oxygen and evens out the mix. If the center never heats, the pile may be too small, too dry, or too brown heavy.

Troubleshooting fast

  • Smells sour or like ammonia: add dry browns, fluff the pile, and turn it.
  • Attracts pests: bury food scraps and finish with a thick brown cap.
  • Dry and inactive: add water, mix in greens, and cover to hold moisture.
  • Slow to finish: chop materials smaller and keep the pile insulated.

When compost is finished

Finished compost is dark, crumbly, and no longer heats when turned. Let it cure for two to four weeks so it becomes stable and gentle on roots. Use it as a 1 to 2 inch top dressing, mix it into new beds, or blend it with potting soil at about one part compost to three parts mix.

Small-space options

If you are short on space, try a lidded bin, a tumbler, or vermicomposting with worms. Trench composting also works well: dig a small trench, add kitchen scraps, cover with soil, and plant on top a few weeks later.

Compost is a practice of attention. Check the feel, the smell, and the heat, and the pile will tell you what it needs. With a few adjustments, you will make soil from scraps and keep waste out of the landfill.
